https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-bur.text: LONDON — Andy Burnham entered Downing Street with a promise to give hard-pressed voters “breathing space” on the cost of living. Now he must show he can deliver. At the top of his list is finding a way to reduce stubbornly high energy bills — even as the Iran-U.S. war forces up prices and ministers are under pressure to cut their own departmental budgets. The new prime minister knows any intervention must make a real impact for voters if he is to turn Labour’s fortunes around. “You need to make an emotional connection with people,” said one senior government official, granted anonymity to talk candidly about Whitehall thinking. Advertisement Advertisement Britain’s new prime minister has already made one bid to show voters he is serious about tackling the problem: Removing VAT from household electricity bills, something he announced on his first day in No. 10 . The move will knock less than £4 off the average monthly bill, ends after one year, and comes with a price tag of £850 million. Downing Street said it will be paid for through so-far unspecified Whitehall savings. But Burnham and his new Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, promised that the intervention is just a start. Cutting VAT is a “ down payment ” ahead of the winter, Fahnbulleh said. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh arrives at 10 Downing Street for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first cabinet meeting, on July 21, 2026 in London, England. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images That means ministers have just weeks before Burnham’s first budget this fall to figure out what, if anything, can really ease the burden — and how to pay for it. Salami slicing “The fiscal space is going to be a challenge, and that is the case for any government,” said Sam Alvis, associate director for environment, energy security, and nature at the Labour-aligned Institute for Public Policy Research think tank. That’s because any intervention to bring down energy bills will have to be funded from already under-pressure Whitehall departments. Advertisement Advertisement “This government is going to have a look at the budget. Whether it chooses to do some priorities differently — that is an open question,” Alvis said. One option for Burnham is to slice more charges from electricity bills, as he did with VAT. But any savings could be quickly wiped out if, as expected, the Middle East crisis pushes up wholesale gas prices. Forecasters at Cornwall Insight predict that average annual household bills will rise by two percent this fall, even after the VAT intervention. That leaves Burnham facing the same problems as the man he replaced, Keir Starmer. Starmer cut £150 off yearly bills last November by shifting some so-called green levies, used to fund a clean energy scheme, onto general taxation. By the summer, that cut had been swallowed up by higher prices driven by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Nonetheless, Alvis said, this approach remains Burnham’s most realistic option. Advertisement Advertisement “We are now in a bit of a scenario of salami slicing, where you're aggregating lots and lots of smaller bits,” he said. “There's no one big thing that you can do that's going to take over £100 off bills. So, it's about accumulating all those things that you think you could possibly do in one go, so it becomes sizable and noticeable.” Decisions, decisions One of those options, proposed by the think tank Nesta and reportedly being considered by Burnham, involves shifting further green levies from electricity bills onto tax. It identified another £42 of savings from a yearly bill, costing the Treasury £1.7 billion per year for a decade. Every small cut helps consumers, insists Andrew Sissons, Nesta’s director of sustainable futures. The think tank has also proposed knocking £22 a year off bills by shifting the standing charge on gas — currently a fixed daily fee — onto the unit rate, which changes depending on how much energy a home uses. That would take a year to implement and would not cost the government a penny, Nesta says. But such moves must be accompanied by larger interventions if voters are to feel the benefit, he added. “The amount you'd need to cut people's energy bills … for it to feel like a real difference is quite substantial,” he said. The government, he argued, should aim for a “big package.” Advertisement Advertisement If the government aims for larger changes, they would come with even greater costs. Nesta has suggested a one-off move to wipe out electricity debt, removing some bailout costs currently funded through bills, taking total annual bill savings to £130. But the Treasury would have to find £2.7 billion to fund that. “[We] shouldn't ignore the fact that there are fiscal trade-offs. But if the government wants to prioritize energy bills, then this is the kind of step it needs to take,” Sissons added, pointing to their proposed levy change alongside the VAT cut. Things take time Net-zero policies will, ministers hope, bring down bills for good. But large-scale changes take years to implement. “Realistically, the only way to deeply, deeply help people is to get them solar panels, is to get them an EV [electric vehicle], potentially heat pumps in some houses as well,” said Alvis. This is another reason to opt for "salami slicing", he said: To “alter the balance of electricity and gas prices, so that those clean technologies stack up and save people even more money.” Advertisement Advertisement Alex Bevan, a research fellow at the Future Governance Forum, agreed that big savings attached to the shift to green energy were still a way off. “There aren't quick workarounds on whichever form of energy you choose to generate and deploy,” he said. But government must nonetheless “lock in the benefits [of clean energy],” he argued. The same official quoted above stressed that no decision had yet been made on how the government would intervene on bills. Asked whether the government favored a series of small policies or one big intervention, they said: “It doesn’t have to be binary. ... It doesn’t have to be one or the other.” A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson said: “The energy secretary’s focus is bringing bills down for good. We will tackle the cost of living to make life's essentials affordable again and bring back hope.” For now, Alvis insisted, Burnham has one thing going for him: He can operate in the knowledge voters accept international issues are pushing up costs. “The political point I would make is: By doing your best effort, you give yourself the space to have a conversation with the public,” he said. https://www.politico.eu/article/us-ceuta.text: The United States on Thursday moved to allay fears that it was questioning Spain’s sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla, but criticized Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s government for its “refusal” to defend the North African exclaves from a “migrant invasion.” Tens of thousands of migrants poured into Ceuta last week from Morocco in a surge that heightened Spanish fears about the vulnerability of its North African cities to hybrid attack . Amid the crisis, Spanish politicians and media raised concerns about the warming relationship between Morocco — which claims Ceuta and Melilla — and the U.S. President Donald Trump, who was infuriated by Socialist Sánchez’s refusal to back the war in Iran . Advertisement Advertisement Many in Madrid expressed fears Washington could decline to rein in Rabat, and pointed to a recent U.S. Congress report that described Ceuta and Melilla as being in “Moroccan territory” and was supportive of negotiations on the “future status” of the cities. But U.S. State Department Spokesperson Tommy Pigott insisted that there has been no change in U.S. policy on the exclaves. “The United States unequivocally supports Spain’s sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla,” he told POLITICO. The State Department noted that the congressional report did not represent U.S. law. Pigott said that allegations suggesting Washington was questioning Spain’s continued control of the cities had been “pushed by nefarious actors who wish to distract from the Spanish government’s shameful refusal to defend its people from the migrant invasion of its territory in Ceuta.” He also argued the Spanish government was solely to blame for the crisis in the exclave, into which 72,000 unauthorized migrants surged last week. “The invasion of tens of thousands of migrants into Ceuta is a direct consequence of the Spanish government’s refusal to defend their sovereignty, secure their borders, and protect their people,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement The crisis in Ceuta initially prompted widespread criticism from EU leaders such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Finnish Interior Minister Mari Rantanen, who last week attacked Spain for having “completely failed to protect the Schengen Area’s external border from infiltration.” Ceuta is not in the Schengen area, and is separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar. While the EU member countries have since reversed course and praised Madrid for its handling of the situation , Pigott on Thursday called on Spain to “take all necessary actions to remove illegal migrants and regain control over its borders.” “Unrestricted mass migration into Ceuta endangers the Spanish people and threatens the security of Europe,” he said. “The State Department stands with the Spanish people and all Europeans in defense of their sovereignty and welcomes all efforts to repel the invasion, remove illegal migrants from European territory, and secure Europe’s borders.”

https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-r.text: Russian leader Vladimir Putin is “in principle” ready for Moscow to resume talks with Washington and Kyiv, the Kremlin said Wednesday. During a meeting in St. Petersburg with U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, Putin said Moscow is ready to restart trilateral negotiations in November, Yuri Ushakov, a senior Putin aide, told reporters . Ushakov added that the “conflict in Ukraine is coming to an end,” and said trilateral talks “ may take place in Abu Dhabi .” Advertisement Advertisement Witkoff confirmed on X that discussions “will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine at the technical level.” His visit was the latest in a new round of U.S. attempts to bring Moscow to the negotiating table to end its war against Ukraine. The special envoy also met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, subsequently announcing a proposal for a three-way leaders’ negotiation. There have been several rounds of talks between the U.S. and Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The most recent discussions stalled in February when the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran. Previous negotiations were largely political theater and failed to yield any broader breakthrough on halting hostilities, prisoner-of-war exchanges or a truce regarding strikes on energy infrastructure. Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported Moscow proposed a potential high-level summit with China and the U.S. to negotiate a deal on ending the war in Ukraine. On Wednesday, footage emerged of Witkoff praising Putin during their face-to-face talks in St. Petersburg, after the Russians released a U.S. prisoner from captivity. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.kyivpost.com/analysis/86315.text: War Ukraine World North America Latin America Europe Eastern Europe Middle East Africa Asia Economy Business Technology Finance Energy Agriculture Videos Podcasts Analysis Corruption Watch Opinions Culture Reviews History Sports Classifieds Spotlight Cartoons EN UK Latvia Elections Russia ANALYSIS: Latvia’s Pro-Ukraine Landslide Hides a Weakness Putin Could Exploit In brief: Latvia’s election gave PM Kulbergs a strong mandate, but just 51.8% of eligible voters participated. For a NATO frontline state bordering Russia and Belarus, the weak turnout highlights concerns about social cohesion and the resilience of its internal defenses. By TVP World Oct. 10, 2026, 12:33 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs holds his son as he talks with the press in front of the polling station in Riga during Latvia’s parliamentary elections on Oct. 3, 2026. (Photo by Wojtek RADWANSKI / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Latvia has just held what its own public broadcaster called “a bit of an embarrassing” election. This bashfulness from Latvia’s National Public Service Broadcaster, LSM, was because only 51.8% of eligible voters turned out, the lowest result since Latvia’s first parliamentary election in the modern era in 1993. Yet those who did turn out handed Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs and his United List 35.3% of the vote and 42 of the 100 seats in the Saeima, Latvia’s parliament – the strongest result achieved by a single political force since Latvia regained independence. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Latvia has emerged from the election with an unusually strong government and an unusually disengaged electorate. Advertisement For most European democracies, that would primarily be a political problem. For Latvia, it is also a security problem. Latvia is a NATO frontline state of just 1.8 million people, bordering both Russia and Belarus. Its grand strategy can be reduced to one overriding objective: make Latvia impossible to isolate. Internationalize survival Latvia cannot deter Russia through mass. It has to do it through connections. That means embedding NATO troops on Latvian soil, keeping the United States and Canada strategically invested in the Baltic region, and integrating more closely with Poland and the Nordic states. It means spending close to 5% of GDP on defense, building fortifications along the eastern frontier, investing in drones and air defense, and reducing Russian economic and informational leverage. Other Topics of Interest Putin Rejects Peace Talks in Trump Call, Vows to Press War Kremlin aide Ushakov said Putin rebuffed talks and vowed to fight on after Trump called with birthday greetings and diesel deals. Above all, it means supporting Ukraine. For Riga, Ukraine is both an ally and a forward school of national defense. The Ukrainian battlefield provides lessons in drones, electronic warfare, air defense and Russian tactics that Latvia hopes never to have to learn for itself. Kulbergs has received a powerful mandate to continue this Atlanticist course. A likely coalition with the National Alliance and New Unity would control 59 seats. Support for Ukraine and NATO remains firmly anchored at the center of the Latvian government. Advertisement But Latvia’s defense strategy also depends on something NATO cannot provide: a cohesive and politically engaged society. Barely half Latvia’s electorate voted, raising uncomfortable questions for a national defence strategy built partly around participation and social cohesion. (Photo: PAP/Abaca) The internal front line Latvia follows an all-of-society approach to defense. Its National Security Concept is explicit that “the existence of the State of Latvia depends on a responsible attitude of all inhabitants of Latvia towards the State and its security.” It links national resilience to the readiness of society as a whole, while defining internal security as resting on a “cohesive civil society” whose citizens participate actively and are prepared to contribute to the defense of the state in a crisis. Advertisement Defense Minister Raivis Melnis put it clearly just over a week before the election: “The real first thing is resilience, which is people and country resilience.” Then almost half of Latvia’s electorate stayed at home. Low turnout does not mean half the country would refuse to defend Latvia. But it does expose weakness in some of the social foundations on which Latvia itself says national resilience depends. President Edgars Rinkēvičs has already drawn attention to the danger. “Disappointment and indifference are dangerous to the democratic foundations and future of our country,” he said after the result. Participation was particularly weak in parts of Latgale, Latvia’s easternmost and most heavily Russian-speaking region. Turnout in Daugavpils, where Russian is dominant in everyday life, was just 46.55%. This takes us to the most sensitive part of Latvia’s security dilemma. Russian-speaking does not mean pro-Russian Almost a quarter of Latvia’s population is ethnically Russian, while Russian is spoken at home by a much larger share. That demographic legacy of the Soviet period has long made Latvia different from Lithuania and has placed questions of language, history and identity close to the center of national politics. Advertisement Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the temptation has been to view this population primarily through the lens of security. The evidence is considerably more complicated. Former Latvian integration minister Nils Muižnieks said: “I do not think that we can talk about a fifth column in Latvia.” Research among Russian-speaking Latvians also suggests that straightforward support for Moscow is a minority position. One major study found 55% supporting neither Russia nor Ukraine. Researcher Mārtiņš Kaprāns argues that this “neutrality cannot be reduced to apathy or ignorance.” Latvia’s parliament has emerged with a stronger governing majority, but record-low turnout raises questions about political engagement beyond its walls. (Photo by Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images) The bigger problem appears to be alienation. Parts of Latvia’s Russian-speaking population have become detached from the country’s mainstream political and media environment. Some distrust Riga. Some dislike policies reducing the public role of the Russian language. Some have become politically homeless following the collapse of Harmony, the party that once dominated Russian-speaking politics. Advertisement This election suggests that the two responses to that alienation are abstention and protest voting. Latvia First and Sovereign Power/Young Latvians, both considerably softer towards Moscow than the governing parties, will together control 32 seats. That does not turn their voters into Kremlin loyalists. But from the perspective of national resilience, alienation is important. The next stage of Latvian security Russia does not need Latvia’s Russian speakers to become a fifth column. A population that distrusts state institutions, withdraws from politics or feels that the Latvian state belongs to somebody else already creates a seam Moscow can exploit. Latvia therefore faces a difficult balancing act. It has good reason to restrict Russian influence, dismantle the remnants of Soviet political power and protect Latvian as the language of the state. At the same time, successful resilience ultimately requires Russian-speaking citizens to feel that they have ownership of that state too. Latvia has spent years hardening its borders, strengthening its military and embedding itself so deeply inside NATO that Moscow could never confront it alone. Advertisement Kulbergs’s landslide gives him an unusually strong mandate to continue that work. The embarrassing part of this election is the reminder that Latvia’s next line of defense has to be built from citizens who believe strongly enough in the Latvian state to participate in it.
